title: Hypertension overview
text: High blood pressure (hypertension) often causes no symptoms and is usually found through routine blood pressure checks. Long-term high blood pressure raises the risk of stroke, heart attack, heart failure and kidney disease. Lifestyle measures include reducing salt intake, regular physical activity, limiting alcohol, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight. Many people also need medication, chosen by a clinician based on age, ethnicity and other conditions. Ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring can help confirm the diagnosis.

title: Type 2 diabetes overview
text: Type 2 diabetes is a condition where the body does not respond properly to insulin or does not make enough insulin, leading to high blood glucose. Common symptoms include thirst, passing urine often, tiredness and blurred vision, although many people have no symptoms. It is commonly diagnosed with an HbA1c blood test. Management usually starts with diet, physical activity and weight management, and metformin is often the first medicine offered. Regular checks of eyes, feet and kidneys help detect complications early.

title: Atrial fibrillation overview
text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an irregular and often fast heart rhythm. Symptoms can include palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness and tiredness, but some people have none. AF increases the risk of stroke because blood clots can form in the heart. Diagnosis is confirmed with an electrocardiogram (ECG). Clinicians assess stroke risk with scoring tools such as CHA2DS2-VASc and may offer anticoagulant medicines to reduce that risk, alongside treatments to control heart rate or rhythm.

title: Electrocardiogram (ECG) basics
text: An electrocardiogram records the electrical activity of the heart using electrodes placed on the skin. A standard 12-lead ECG shows waves labelled P, QRS and T, which reflect atrial depolarisation, ventricular depolarisation and ventricular repolarisation. ECGs help detect arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, signs of heart attack, and conduction problems. Machine learning models trained on large ECG datasets can classify rhythms automatically, but their outputs still need clinical review.

title: Asthma overview
text: Asthma is a long-term condition affecting the airways, causing wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough. Symptoms often vary over time and can be triggered by allergens, infections, exercise or cold air. Diagnosis may involve spirometry and other lung function tests. Treatment usually includes inhaled medicines: relievers for quick symptom relief and preventers, often containing inhaled corticosteroids, to reduce airway inflammation. A personal asthma action plan helps people manage flare-ups.

title: Sepsis warning signs
text: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection in which the body's response damages its own tissues and organs. Warning signs can include high or low temperature, fast breathing, fast heart rate, confusion, mottled or discoloured skin, and passing little urine. Sepsis is a medical emergency and needs urgent assessment. Early warning scores such as NEWS2 are used in UK hospitals to help staff recognise patients who are deteriorating.

title: Chronic kidney disease overview
text: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a long-term reduction in kidney function. It is often found through blood tests measuring estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urine tests for albumin. High blood pressure and diabetes are the most common causes. Early CKD usually has no symptoms. Management focuses on controlling blood pressure and blood glucose, reviewing medicines that may affect the kidneys, and monitoring kidney function over time.

title: Clinical AI safety principles
text: Clinical AI systems should be evaluated on data that represents the patients they will be used with, because performance can drop when populations differ. Important practices include measuring accuracy across subgroups, keeping a human clinician in the loop, logging model outputs for audit, and monitoring performance after deployment. In the UK, software that informs diagnosis or treatment may be regulated as a medical device by the MHRA.
